title: You’ve been trained to spot the obvious sins.
paragraphs: You’ve been trained to spot the obvious sins.

The loud ones.
The scandalous ones.
The ones that make headlines and whispers.

But the ones that sat comfortably in church…
the ones dressed in Scripture, speaking in polished prayers…
Those were the ones Jesus confronted the hardest.

Not the prostitutes.
Not the tax collectors.
Not the broken people everyone else avoided.
It was the religious.

The clean-looking ones.
The disciplined ones.
The ones who knew the Bible but didn’t know God.
And that should shake you more than you think.
Because it means you can look right… and still be completely wrong.
There’s a moment that doesn’t get talked about enough.
Jesus sitting across from a group of religious leaders—men who fasted, tithed, prayed publicly, memorized Scripture—and instead of affirming them…
He dismantled them.

“Woe to you, teachers of the law and Pharisees, you hypocrites!
You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence.” (Matthew 23:25)
Read that again.
They looked clean.
But God wasn’t looking at what people saw.
God saw it.

He saw the hidden pride.
The quiet superiority.
The internal applause when they compared themselves to others.
And Jesus didn’t soften it.
He exposed it.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Religious pride is more dangerous than obvious sin because it hides itself as righteousness.
The sinner knows they’re broken.
The proud person thinks they’re fine.
One cries out for mercy.
The other silently thanks God they’re not like “those people.”
You’ve heard that prayer before.
“God, I thank You that I’m not like other men…” (Luke 18:11)
It sounds spiritual.
But it disgusted Jesus.
Because it wasn’t worship.
It was self-worship wearing God’s name.
And this is where it turns personal.
You didn’t say it out loud.
But you thought it.

When you saw someone fall into sin…
When you noticed someone less disciplined…
When you compared your habits, your consistency, your “walk”…
You felt it.
That quiet lift inside your chest.
That subtle sense that you’re doing better.
You knew.
Jesus tells a story about two men praying.
One religious. One broken.
The religious man lists his achievements.
The other can barely lift his head.
“God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” (Luke 18:13)
And Jesus says something that flips everything:
“I tell you, this man, rather than the other, went home justified before God.” (Luke 18:14)
Not the disciplined one.
Not the outwardly righteous one.
The one who knew he needed mercy.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
This is why Jesus rebuked religious pride so sharply.
Because it blocks repentance.
And without repentance… there is no salvation.
You can’t be filled with grace if you’re already full of yourself.
You can’t receive a Savior if you don’t think you need saving.
And that’s the trap.
Not sin alone…
But thinking you’ve outgrown the need for grace.
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
Opposes.
Not ignores.
Not delays.
Opposes.
That means the greatest resistance in your spiritual life might not be the devil…
It might be your own pride.
But there’s still mercy.
Because Jesus didn’t just rebuke.
He invited.
Even the Pharisees weren’t beyond grace—if they would just come low.

If they would drop the image…
stop performing…
and admit what God already sees.
Because at the cross, there are no “better sinners.”
Only forgiven ones.
This is where everything shifts.
You can keep managing appearances…
Or you can finally surrender the truth.
One path keeps you respected.
The other makes you free.
Say it plainly.
“I need grace too.”
Not later.
Now.
Because the longer pride stays hidden… the harder your heart becomes.
Stay with this. Go deeper than surface faith.
Follow this path if you’re done pretending and ready to walk in truth daily.
And if you know someone who looks “fine” on the outside but is drifting inside… send this to them. Not to judge them. To wake them.
Let it sit with you. Come back to it when pride tries to creep in quietly again.
And if conviction is real, don’t hide it—say something. Even if it’s just: “Lord, humble me.”
